SATOM 1.12.0

Policy cloning now copies SNI policies, certificates and profile settings it used to miss, and a declined section is finally left exactly as the destination had it.

👤 ForViewerOperatorAdministratorAdvanced user
On this page

  • What's new

  • Cloning: backend reachability check

Released: 2026-08-22 · All releases

In short#

This release is about policy cloning. A clone or migration now carries several things it used to leave behind — SNI policies, certificate material, references to trigger policies and custom responses — and it compares a profile's own settings, not just its lists. It also fixes an important flaw: when you declined a section, the profile that pointed at it could still be written with the source's value. Operators who clone or migrate server policies will notice the difference most; administrators get a new sizing guide and a clearer message when a node runs out of disk.

What's new#

Cloning: things that are now copied#

SNI policies. An SNI policy used to be treated like a certificate and skipped, so its member rows were skipped too and the copy arrived pointing at an SNI table the destination had never seen. SNI policies and their rows are now created at the destination like any other object.

Certificate material. Certificates and their private keys cannot be read through the appliance's web API, so SATOM now carries them over its SSH connection as part of the clone.

  • They are copied before the first write, because a certificate is something other objects depend on. Discovering a missing certificate halfway through an apply would leave you already committed.
  • A certificate name the destination already has is left alone.
  • The private key never appears in a plan, a report or a log.

Trigger policies and custom responses. Many objects name a log trigger policy, and a Web Protection Profile can also name a custom response page and a quarantined-IP trigger next to its redirect URL. Nothing used to create these on the destination, so an appliance that lacked them refused the whole object or profile — every setting was lost with it. (This was first reported as "the redirect URL is not being cloned"; the redirect URL itself always travelled, it was its neighbours that broke the save.) These references are now part of the clone wherever they occur.

Cloning: compare a profile and decide#

There is a third choice for how a clone treats a profile: New, compare and decide. Until now SATOM compared the rows inside a profile's lists but never the profile's own switches, so a profile whose lists matched but whose settings differed looked identical when it was not. With this choice the profile itself is compared, and you decide what happens. Nothing is pre-ticked.

Cloning: reuse a destination profile, or create one only if missing#

Two new options, available both in the single-policy clone dialog and in bulk jobs:

  • Reuse a profile that already exists on the destination instead of creating a new one.
  • Create the profile only if it is missing on the destination.

In a bulk run each profile is handled once per pair of source profile and landing profile, so the same profile is not created repeatedly.

Cloning: rows the destination already has are updated, not duplicated#

The appliance treats some rows as duplicates when a few key values match, even if the rest of the row differs. SATOM used to see such a row as missing and plan to create it; the appliance then refused the duplicate and kept serving the old value. Matching rows are now reconciled — updated in place — instead of re-created.

Cloning: backend reachability check#

A pre-flight check can now test whether the backend servers are reachable, from two places that are always reported separately: from the destination appliance, and from the SATOM node itself. A result that could not be determined is shown as unknown, never folded into "reachable" (which would hide a real outage) or "down" (which would invent one). The check is off by default.

Cloning: faster pre-flight analysis#

Pre-flight analysis of several policies now runs in parallel. In a measured run of 10 policies it went from about 51 seconds to about 21 seconds, with the same plan.

Sizing guide#

The manual has a new sizing guide. The old requirement tables only stated the minimum the installer needs; they never said how large a node must be for the number of devices it manages. Key points:

  • Device polling is the limit, not storage. A node spends a little under a second per device in each 3-minute collection cycle, which puts about 110 devices on one installation at a 50 % load.
  • Configuration history grows faster than metrics — roughly twice as fast — because metric samples are extremely compact.
  • The installation guide now says its table is a minimum and links to the sizing tiers, and the user guide mentions it where you edit the collection intervals that affect it.

A clearer message when a node runs out of disk#

The alert engine records and sends every finding through the database, so it can never warn you about a full disk that has taken the database down. When it now fails, it writes the node's disk, memory and load figures to the system log, so the cause is visible there. This makes the failure readable; it does not prevent it — free disk space still has to be watched from outside the node.

What changes for you#

  • Declining a section now really keeps the destination's version. Previously, declining a section removed it from the plan, but the profile that pointed at it was still written with the source's value. The destination then pointed at something it did not have, and the appliance replaced it with a default of its own — so you got neither the source's nor the destination's setting. Now:
  • if the item that points at the declined section already exists on the destination, that reference is put back to the value the destination has today;
  • if that item would be newly created, there is nothing to keep, so it is dropped from the plan too — along with anything that depends on it — and the report names it.
  • A row is dropped when its parent object is declined. A row whose parent you declined used to stay in the plan and be written against an object that was never going to exist. Two unrelated objects that happen to share a name no longer affect each other's rows.

Fixed#

  • Saving an FTP server policy was always refused. Every valid FTP server-policy save came back saying the firmware has no FTP protection profile collection. Collections the appliance's web API cannot read now produce an "unverified" warning instead of a refusal.
  • Certificate import failed on appliances with ADOMs enabled. On an ADOM-enabled appliance the first step of the certificate import was rejected, and the rest of the import was then sent to whatever prompt happened to be active. The import now enters the right place on both kinds of appliance.
  • The Sentinel button that arms an automatic blocking response always failed with "your session expired or the form was stale". It now works.
  • Sentinel could not be found in search or on the Concept Map, because five of its pages were missing from the map. They are now mapped.
  • Three clone options sent from the browser were ignored. Reusing a destination profile, creating a profile only if missing, and reconciling rows never reached the clone engine from the web page, so the run silently used the defaults. They are now honoured.
  • Putting a declined value back could find nothing to restore, because the destination's current value was read too late. It is now read at the moment the decision is made.
  • A decision about one profile could pull in an item from outside that profile that merely had identical values. Items are now matched exactly.

Under the hood#

  • Internal device names were removed from comments in shipped files.
  • Sample private-key text in a placeholder and in test files is now assembled at runtime, so the release publisher's secret scanner no longer stops on it.
  • The manual's counts were corrected: Settings has 26 panels (Vault and Sentinel were missing from the count), and the Concept Map maps 88 pages and excludes 112.
